_about: Bibliography. Every species record cites the sources it draws on by id; this file resolves those ids to full references.
_rights: The descriptive writing on this site is original. The species portraits are historical illustrations in the public domain, credited under every plate. Conservation status, trend, range and most population figures restate data from the sources listed below, chiefly the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species, and every species record names the sources it draws on. Those data belong to their publishers and stay subject to their terms: the IUCN Red List Terms and Conditions of Use permit use for conservation, education and research, and forbid commercial use — which they define to include any use by or on behalf of a for-profit entity — without IUCN’s written permission. This archive is non-commercial: it carries no advertising, sells nothing, takes no sponsorship or affiliate revenue, and is published for education and conservation. Anyone reusing the data here is bound by the same terms.

sources.title: The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
sources.publisher: International Union for Conservation of Nature
sources.note: The backbone of this archive. Categories, population trends and range countries come from each taxon's current Red List assessment, and the year shown is the year that assessment was published. Where the IUCN has not assessed a taxon separately, the record says so and names the national or regional list used instead. Cite as: IUCN 2026. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Version 2026-1. https://www.iucnredlist.org. Accessed 14–15 September 2026, and every record re-read against the Red List API on 10 November 2026, when all 273 that can be keyed by name still agreed.

sources.title: BirdLife International bird assessments
sources.note: BirdLife International is the IUCN Red List Authority for birds: it compiles the assessment for every bird species and IUCN publishes it on the Red List. The bird categories, years, trends and population figures in this archive were read from those Red List assessment pages. They were not taken from BirdLife's Data Zone, whose terms do not permit automated access, and nothing here is copied from it.

sources.title: NatureServe Explorer
sources.note: Source of the G1-G5 global conservation ranks shown for North American species. G1 means critically imperilled; G5 means demonstrably secure. Sub-ranks such as G5T1 apply the scale to a subspecies.

sources.title: Environmental Conservation Online System (ECOS)
sources.note: Authoritative source for United States Endangered Species Act listing status, critical habitat designations and the annual species status reports quoted for condors, ferrets and red wolves.

sources.title: Threatened and Endangered Species Directory
sources.note: ESA listings and stock assessments for marine species in United States waters, including the North Atlantic right whale, Rice's whale and smalltooth sawfish counts.

sources.title: COSEWIC Wildlife Species Assessments
sources.publisher: Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada
sources.note: Canadian national assessments underlying the Species at Risk Act (SARA) statuses shown for Canadian species.

sources.title: Red List of South African Species
sources.note: National assessments for South African species, used alongside the global Red List for the African penguin, riverine rabbit, Cape parrot and geometric tortoise.

sources.title: Livro Vermelho da Fauna Brasileira Ameaçada de Extinção
sources.publisher: ICMBio / Ministério do Meio Ambiente, Brazil
sources.note: Brazil's national red book. Provides the Portuguese-language national categories shown for Brazilian species, which sometimes differ from the global Red List.

sources.title: Threatened Species and Ecological Communities
sources.publisher: Australian Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water
sources.note: Listings under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999. Shown where the Australian national category differs from the global one, as it does for the koala.

sources.title: New Zealand Threat Classification System
sources.note: The national classification (Nationally Critical, Nationally Endangered, and so on) and the recovery programme counts for kākāpō, takahē and Māui dolphin.

sources.title: European Red List of Species
sources.note: Regional assessments for Europe. A species can be Least Concern globally and Endangered in Europe; where that is so, both are shown.

sources.title: Council Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora
sources.note: The legal instrument behind European species protection. Referenced where Annex II or IV listing is the operative protection for a species.

sources.title: CITES Appendices I, II and III
sources.publisher: Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora
sources.note: Governs international trade. Appendix I effectively bans commercial trade. Cited for every species whose principal threat is trafficking.

sources.title: Appendices of the Convention on Migratory Species
sources.note: The Bonn Convention. Cited for migratory species — sharks, albatrosses, the Siberian crane — whose protection requires agreement between range states.

sources.title: Conservation Measures and Fishery Reports
sources.publisher: Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources
sources.note: The body that manages the Southern Ocean krill and toothfish fisheries. Source for the fishery context around emperor penguins and Antarctic whales.

sources.title: Stock Assessment and Management Procedure Reports
sources.publisher: Commission for the Conservation of Southern Bluefin Tuna
sources.note: Provides the spawning stock biomass estimates behind the southern bluefin tuna's rebuilding trajectory.

sources.title: Species Assessments
sources.publisher: Agreement on the Conservation of Albatrosses and Petrels
sources.note: Population and bycatch data for albatrosses and large petrels across the Southern Ocean.

sources.title: Flyway Site Network and Waterbird Population Estimates
sources.note: Source for intertidal habitat loss along the Yellow Sea and the counts behind the spoon-billed sandpiper's decline.

sources.title: IUCN SSC Cat Specialist Group
sources.note: The volunteer expert network that produces the Red List assessments for wild cats. Population figures attributed to a 'Specialist Group' in this archive come from its published assessments and action plans.

sources.title: IUCN SSC Canid Specialist Group
sources.note: The volunteer expert network that produces the Red List assessments for wild dogs, wolves and foxes. Population figures attributed to a 'Specialist Group' in this archive come from its published assessments and action plans.

sources.title: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group
sources.note: The volunteer expert network that produces the Red List assessments for primates. Population figures attributed to a 'Specialist Group' in this archive come from its published assessments and action plans. The group's own site at primate-sg.org currently serves a certificate that does not match its hostname, so this entry points at the parent commission instead.

sources.title: African Rhino Specialist Group continental estimates
sources.note: The body that compiles the official continental black and white rhino totals reported to CITES. Source for both rhino counts here.

sources.title: Asian Rhino Specialist Group assessments
sources.note: Compiles the Javan, Sumatran and greater one-horned rhino figures with the Indonesian, Indian and Nepali governments.

sources.title: African Elephant Status Report and African Elephant Database
sources.publisher: IUCN SSC African Elephant Specialist Group
sources.note: The continental elephant database, incorporating the Great Elephant Census aerial survey of 18 countries.

sources.title: IUCN SSC Asian Elephant Specialist Group
sources.note: Range-state population synthesis for the Asian elephant and its subspecies.

sources.title: Africa's Giraffe: A Conservation Guide and country assessments
sources.note: The only organisation producing range-wide giraffe numbers by subspecies; source for the Nubian and reticulated giraffe figures.

sources.title: Global Tiger Forum national estimate compilation
sources.note: Aggregates national tiger census results from the thirteen range states into the global wild tiger figure.

sources.title: Reports of the International Committee for the Recovery of the Vaquita (CIRVA)
sources.note: The acoustic and visual survey series that produces the vaquita count each year — the reason the figure can be stated to single digits.

sources.title: Sahara Conservation field survey reports
sources.note: Aerial and ground surveys for addax, dama gazelle, scimitar-horned oryx and Saharan cheetah in Niger and Chad.

sources.title: SAVE — Saving Asia's Vultures from Extinction
sources.note: Coordinates the road-transect monitoring and the vulture safe zone programme behind the South Asian vulture figures.

sources.title: Lemur Conservation Strategy and Action Plan
sources.publisher: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group and partners
sources.note: The costed action plan for all lemur species, and the reference for site-level lemur population estimates.

sources.title: Primates in Peril: The World's 25 Most Endangered Primates
sources.publisher: IUCN SSC Primate Specialist Group, IPS and Re:wild
sources.note: The biennial listing that flags the primates closest to extinction. Species carrying this citation have appeared on a recent edition. The group's own site at primate-sg.org currently serves a certificate that does not match its hostname, so this entry points at the parent commission instead.

sources.title: AmphibiaWeb
sources.note: Species accounts, chytrid fungus distribution and decline records for every amphibian in this archive.

sources.title: GlobalTree Portal and ThreatSearch
sources.note: The conservation status of the world's tree species, used for the baobab, monkey puzzle, Wollemi pine and Lebanon cedar.

sources.title: EDGE of Existence species list
sources.note: Ranks species by Evolutionary Distinctiveness combined with Global Endangerment. Cited for species with no close living relatives, such as the kagu, aye-aye and Amami rabbit.

sources.title: IUCN Red List assessment: Saola (Pseudoryx nghetinhensis)
sources.publisher: Timmins, R.J., Hedges, S. & Robichaud, W. 2020. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2020: e.T18597A166485696 (amended version of 2016 assessment)
sources.note: Critically Endangered A2acd+3cd+4acd; C2a(i), assessed 27 November 2015: 25–750 mature individuals, best estimate 50–300. The IUCN annotates the assessment as needing updating. Checked against Red List version 2026-1 on 14 September 2026.

sources.title: IUCN Red List assessment: Panamanian golden frog (Atelopus zeteki)
sources.publisher: IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group. 2019. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2019: e.T54563A54341110
sources.note: Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) A2acde; D, assessed 23 May 2018: 0–49 mature individuals and no known location. Checked against Red List version 2026-1 on 14 September 2026.

sources.title: IUCN Red List assessment: ʻAkikiki (Oreomystis bairdi)
sources.publisher: BirdLife International. 2018. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2018: e.T22720809A130843089
sources.note: Critically Endangered C2a(ii), assessed 14 August 2018 on a 2012 estimate of 150–610 mature individuals, before the wild population collapsed. Checked against Red List version 2026-1 and the BirdLife Data Zone on 14 September 2026.

sources.title: IUCN Red List assessment: South China tiger (Panthera tigris ssp. amoyensis)
sources.publisher: Nyhus, P. 2008. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2008: e.T15965A5334628
sources.note: Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct in the Wild) D, assessed 30 June 2008. Still published as the subspecies' own listing, separate from the Endangered listing of the tiger as a species, and annotated by the IUCN as needing updating. Checked against Red List version 2026-1 on 14 September 2026.

sources.title: Panamanian Golden Frog
sources.publisher: Panama Amphibian Rescue and Conservation Project
sources.note: Source for chytridiomycosis reaching El Valle de Antón in 2006, the last wild record in 2009, the 2010 law making the frog a national symbol, and the captive population of more than 1,000 adults at over 50 US and Canadian institutions.

sources.title: Scientists Trial Reintroductions of Panamanian Golden Frogs
sources.publisher: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, 25 February 2026
sources.note: Reports the trial in which 100 captive-bred golden frogs were held for 12 weeks in soft-release pens in Panama before many of the survivors were fully released.

sources.title: Captive-bred Panamanian golden frogs released to the wild
sources.note: Source for about 70% of the frogs in the release trial dying of chytridiomycosis during their 12 weeks in pens.

sources.title: Saving Kauaʻi Forest Birds
sources.publisher: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, 13 October 2023
sources.note: Reports that Kauaʻi Forest Bird Recovery Project surveys detected only five ʻakikiki remaining in the wild, and that avian malaria spread by the non-native southern house mosquito is the main threat to Hawaiian honeycreepers.

sources.title: Kauaʻi County Council honors Pakele, the last known wild ʻakikiki on Garden Isle
sources.note: Source for the last sighting of the last known wild ʻakikiki, a female named Pakele, on 29 August 2025, and for the species surviving in a conservation breeding flock operated by San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance.

sources.title: Dramatic decline of wild South China tigers Panthera tigris amoyensis: field survey of priority tiger reserves
sources.publisher: Tilson, R., Defu, H., Muntifering, J. & Nyhus, P.J. 2004. Oryx 38
sources.note: Sino-American field surveys in 2001 and 2002 of eight reserves in five provinces, chosen as the habitat most likely to hold tigers, found no evidence of wild South China tigers and few prey species.

sources.title: Population genomic analysis provides evidence of the past success and future potential of South China tiger captive conservation
sources.publisher: Wang, C., Wu, D.-D., Yuan, Y.-H. et al. 2023. BMC Biology 21
sources.note: Source for the South China tiger surviving only in zoos, with every living animal descended from two male and four female wild-caught tigers.

sources.title: To track a unicorn: Laos team goes all out to find the last saolas
sources.note: Source for the Saola Foundation's search of 300 km² of Bolikhamxay province, Laos, with detection dogs and rapid DNA testing from April 2025, and for a 2013 camera-trap photograph in central Vietnam being the last confirmed record.

sources.title: Year of the Forest Birds marked changes for birds, hope for the future
sources.publisher: Hawaiʻi Department of Land and Natural Resources, 19 December 2024
sources.note: Source for the ʻakikiki being considered functionally extinct in the wild at the end of 2024, with five or fewer wild birds remaining.

sources.title: IUCN SSC experts urge immediate action to find Saola before it's too late
sources.publisher: International Union for Conservation of Nature, 20 August 2021
sources.note: Source for the saola's discovery by Western science in 1992, snaring as a major threat, no conclusive detection since 2013, and expert estimates of fewer than 100 individuals.

sources.title: Mongolian Red List of Mammals
sources.publisher: Clark, E.L., Munkhbat, J., Dulamtseren, S., Baillie, J.E.M., Batsaikhan, N., Samiya, R. & Stubbe, M. (compilers) 2006. Regional Red List Series Vol. 1, Zoological Society of London
sources.note: Regional assessment using IUCN categories and criteria. Lists the Gobi bear (Ursus arctos gobiensis) as Critically Endangered under criterion D. Checked on nationalredlist.org on 15 September 2026.

sources.title: Lista Rossa IUCN dei vertebrati italiani
sources.publisher: Comitato Italiano IUCN and Ministero dell’Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica
sources.note: National assessment using IUCN categories and criteria. Lists the Marsican brown bear (Ursus arctos marsicanus) as Critically Endangered, C2a(i,ii); D. Checked on iucn.it on 15 September 2026.

sources.title: Can a new DNA test save the world’s rarest turtle?
sources.note: Reports that two or three Yangtze giant softshell turtles are known (Suzhou Zoo, Xuan Khanh lake and possibly Dong Mo lake) after the last known female died at Dong Mo in April 2023.
